title: Running and Tracking a Training Job
intro: Model training in production usually runs as a Kubernetes Job, with MLflow tracking the results — let's walk through both.

steps.prompt: Set the MLflow tracking URI to your tracking server.
steps.explanation: This tells your training script where to log metrics/params/artifacts — usually set once per environment.
steps.why: MLflow reads this environment variable automatically inside your training code — the alternative is hardcoding the tracking URI in every script, which breaks the moment you move from local to a shared staging server.

steps.prompt: Launch the training job as a Kubernetes Job named 'train-run-01', using image 'my-training-image' and running 'python train.py'.
expected_commands: kubectl create job train-run-01 --image=my-training-image -- python train.py
steps.explanation: Running training as a Job (not a Deployment) makes sense because it's meant to run once to completion, not stay running forever.
steps.why: A Deployment would restart the training container forever every time it finished — a Job specifically tracks completion and stops, which is the correct lifecycle for something meant to run once and produce a result, not serve traffic indefinitely.

steps.prompt: Follow its logs to watch training progress.
steps.fake_output:
Epoch 1/10 - loss: 0.842 - accuracy: 0.71
Epoch 2/10 - loss: 0.601 - accuracy: 0.79
...
Training complete. Model saved.
steps.explanation: Same kubectl logs you already know — training jobs are just regular pods under the hood.
steps.why: 'job/train-run-01' works here the same way 'deployment/web' does elsewhere — kubectl resolves it to the pod the Job created, so you don't need to know the pod's actual generated name to follow its logs.

steps.explanation: 1/1 completions means the job's pod exited with code 0 — success.
steps.why: Watching the logs stream 'Training complete' is reassuring but isn't proof of a clean exit code — 'get jobs' is the authoritative source, since a script can print a success-looking message and still exit non-zero due to a bug in its own cleanup code.

steps.prompt: List experiments logged in MLflow to confirm this run was tracked.
steps.explanation: Every training run's params, metrics, and model artifact get logged here — this is what makes 'which model version is this' answerable months later.
steps.why: This is the MLOps-specific step that a plain Kubernetes Job wouldn't give you on its own — the Job confirms the code ran, but MLflow is what actually answers 'what hyperparameters and accuracy did this specific run produce,' which is the part that matters for reproducibility.
